source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter II, §9 A Cardinal Principle, Example 22

steps.title: The free pawn
steps.source: In the position shown above, White can draw by playing P - Kt 4, according to the general rule that governs such cases, i.e., to advance the Pawn that is free from opposition.

narration.say: Two pawns against one on the queen side.
White draws with b4: the rule from Chapter One, push the pawn that has no pawn opposing it.
But suppose White plays a4 instead.

feedback.a6: Close, but go further: with the pawn on a5, b4 can always be met by a capture.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Stop both white pawns with one.
exercise.hint: The black a-pawn goes two squares.
exercise.success: 1...a5. One black pawn now holds two white ones.

steps.title: One of the cardinal principles
steps.source: Then Black can win by playing 1...P - Q R 4, applying one of the cardinal principles of the high strategy of chess: A unit that holds two. […] It constitutes one of the principal weapons in the hands of a master.

narration.say: A unit that holds two. It is one of the cardinal principles of chess strategy.
The white b-pawn can never pass freely. Now watch the main line.
The black king goes to f4. Best.
Pawn to b4, and Black takes. Best.
Both sides run: a5, b3; a6, b2; a7, b1 queen; a8 queen.

feedback.*: Look for a check that also attacks the queen on a8, on the same line.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Both sides have a queen. Find the skewer.
exercise.wrong: Look for a check that also attacks the queen on a8, on the same line.
exercise.hint: The queen checks from e4, on the long diagonal.

steps.title: A classical ending
steps.source: This brings the game to a position which is won by Black, and which constitutes one of the classical endings of King and Pawns.

narration.say: This king and pawn ending is won for Black. It is one of the classical endings, and it is the next lesson.
